opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny, because in hindsight I think a lot of what we were doing with language GANs during my PhD was really a precursor to RLHF, even if we didn't frame it that way at the time. The core idea was the same: you have a generator, the language model, and instead of training it only with teacher forcing on maximum likelihood, you want some signal that tells it how good a whole generated sequence is. In a GAN, that signal comes from a discriminator. In RLHF, it comes from a reward model trained on human preferences. But structurally, both are a learned critic plus policy-gradient-style optimization of a model that samples text.

And we ran into all the same problems. Text is discrete, so you can't just backprop through the sampling, and you end up with REINFORCE-style estimators that have high variance and are very unstable. You get mode collapse, where the generator finds a few outputs that fool the discriminator and just repeats them, which is basically what we now call reward hacking. That's also why we spent a lot of time on things like the exploration/exploitation trade-off and on how temperature and sampling affect quality versus diversity. Some of our work showed that once you account for that trade-off properly, a well-tuned MLE model with the right decoding was often as good as a GAN, which was a bit humbling.

What changed with RLHF, I think, comes down to two things. First, the discriminator was always chasing a moving target, and it learned to tell "real" from "fake" text, which isn't really what you care about. A reward model trained on human preferences gives you a signal aligned with what you actually want: helpfulness, correctness, following instructions. Second, scale. We were doing this with small models trained from scratch or barely pretrained. When you start from a strong pretrained and instruction-tuned model, the policy already produces reasonable text, so RL only has to steer it, not teach it language. That makes the optimization far more stable, especially with a KL penalty that keeps you close to the original model, which plays the same role our tricks for avoiding collapse were trying to play.

So I see it as a continuity. The intuition that you need to go beyond imitation, that the model should learn from feedback on its own samples rather than only copying human text, was right. We just didn't have the right reward signal or the right starting point yet. And honestly, one of the things that convinced me RLHF was so important for Llama 2 was exactly this: with supervised data alone you're capped by the quality of the human demonstrations, but humans are much better at comparing two answers than writing the perfect one. Feedback on samples lets the model go beyond the annotators, and that's the promise language GANs had and couldn't quite deliver.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually a fun one for me, because when I look back at my PhD work on language GANs, it's really the same problem we're solving today with RLHF, just with the wrong tools and the wrong scale.

The motivation back then was identical. You train a model with teacher forcing, maximum likelihood on next-token prediction, and you get this exposure bias problem: at training time the model always sees the gold prefix, but at inference time it has to condition on its own generations, and errors compound. So the idea was, okay, let's get a learned signal on the full generated sequence instead of a per-token likelihood. And the natural thing to do, coming from the vision world in 2017, 2018, was a GAN. You have a discriminator that looks at a whole sample and says real or fake, and that becomes your reward for the generator.

But text is discrete, so you can't backprop through the sampling step. So what did everyone do? Policy gradient. REINFORCE, or some variant. Which means a language GAN is literally a generator trained with RL, where the reward model is a discriminator that is itself learning. If you squint, that's RLHF with a learned reward model, except the reward model is trained to distinguish human text from model text rather than trained on human preferences.

And it didn't work very well, honestly. There was a famous paper, "Language GANs Falling Short," showing that if you just tune the temperature on an MLE model you beat most of the GAN approaches on the quality-diversity tradeoff. We did some things to improve it, like SelfGAN, where you use the discriminator inside the decoding process rather than only as a training signal. But fundamentally we were fighting three things at once: a tiny generator, a discriminator with no real understanding of language, and an unstable adversarial game where the reward is a moving target.

What changed with RLHF is not the algorithm. It's the ingredients. First, the pretrained model is enormous and already very good, so the policy starts in a reasonable region and you're refining rather than learning from scratch. Second, the reward model is also a huge pretrained model, so it actually captures something meaningful about what "good" means. And third, you replace the adversarial signal with human preferences, which is a fixed target, plus the KL penalty to the reference model so you don't drift off a cliff. That stability was exactly what we didn't have.

So the way I see it, language GANs were the right intuition, that you need a sequence-level learned reward and an RL loop to optimize against it, but they were five years early and three orders of magnitude too small. When I was working on Llama 2 and we saw how much RLHF was doing, it felt very familiar. The humbling part is realizing the key insight wasn't a clever loss function, it was scale and better data for the reward.

r001.rationale: The response describes the discriminator as a learned reward signal distinguishing human text from model text, analogous to an RLHF reward model but without human preference training.

astra-6.text:
I see a pretty direct connection. When I was working on GANs for language, the difficulty was that text is discrete: you can’t just backpropagate through a sampled word. So you use reinforcement learning. The language model generates a sequence, the discriminator gives it a score, and that score becomes a reward for updating the model.

If you look at RLHF, the structure is very similar. You have a language model generating text, a reward model scoring it, and reinforcement learning to improve the language model. The important difference is what the score represents. In a GAN, the discriminator is trying to distinguish generated text from real text. In RLHF, the reward model is trained to capture human preferences. So you move from “Does this look like the training data?” to “Is this an answer a human would prefer?”

They’re not exactly the same algorithm, but conceptually, that earlier work was very close to the machinery we now use for alignment.

r001.rationale: The response says the GAN discriminator scores text by distinguishing generated text from real text, and contrasts that with an RLHF reward model trained on human preferences. It does not describe the discriminator as a synthetic substitute for human feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
I see a pretty direct connection. With language GANs, we were training a discriminator to distinguish generated text from human text, and then using its signal to improve the generator. Because text is discrete, you couldn’t simply backpropagate through the sampled tokens, so we used reinforcement learning.

With RLHF, you also learn a model that provides a reward, and then optimize the language model against that reward. The important difference is what you’re asking the reward model to capture: instead of “Does this look like human text?” it’s “Which response does a human prefer?” Those aren’t the same objective. A response can look very human and still be unhelpful.

So I wouldn’t say language GANs and RLHF are identical, but there’s a shared idea: learning the training signal rather than specifying it by hand, and using reinforcement learning to turn that signal into better generation.
